description.narrative:
In Gaza Province, floods affected 600K+ ppl <(>&<)> displaced 392K (IOM DTM ‘26). Impact is exacerbated by existing poverty rate (70-80%, UNDP ‘24). Risk index data shows coping capacity score of only 6.7/10, meaning that HH already exhausted their ability to manage shocks before the floods. RNA conducted in end Jan. by HPP members confirmed critical hum. needs. HH report near total crop loss(>90%), eliminating both food sources <(>&<)> income. Families lost on average 2–4 livestock, removing their primary financial safety net. Flooded roads have disrupted market access, <(>&<)> HH report that food prices have increased sharply (30–50%). FGDs confirmed HH have reduced meals to 1–2/day. Many homes are severely/completely destroyed. Displaced families take refuge in overcrowded schools <(>&<)> accommodation centres with minimal privacy <(>&<)> protection. Contaminated water sources pose a critical health risk. 95% of boreholes <(>&<)> wells are flooded <(>&<)> sanitation facilities in resettlement centres are overstretched (ratios up to 1:100), heightening cholera <(>&<)> other waterborne diseases risk. Serious protection concerns were reported. Communities face emotional distress, exposure to violence <(>&<)> barriers to assistance, esp. for PWD. Women in 14 FGDs raised serious safety concerns, incl. GBV, in resettlement centres due to lack of lighting, lockable shelters <(>&<)> gender-segregated latrines, creating conditions for violence <(>&<)> abuse in overcrowded sites. Loss of civil documentation (reported in 16 FGDs) further restricts access to services. Despite ongoing hum. efforts, major gaps remain. Water infrastructure is damaged, sanitation insufficient, hygiene materials scarce <(>&<)> accessible WASH facilities for PWD largely absent. Protection mechanisms/GBV referral are weak. Oxfam <(>&<)> AJOAGO propose a WASH <(>&<)> Protection Action through DRA, complemented w/ FSL via own funding in Mabalane, Mapai <(>&<)> Massangena districts (Gaza Province). These locations have limited responders, are hard to reach <(>&<)> were selected w/ DRA partners.
Delivery model is hybrid w/ Oxfam providing coordination, technical oversight, fiduciary mgt <(>&<)> quality assurance. Oxfam <(>&<)> AJOAGO are working together based on their established presence, access, proven response capacity <(>&<)> previous collaborations. Oxfam has started its flood response through internal funds. AJOAGO was actively involved in the RNA, <(>&<)> in the identification of priority needs <(>&<)> selection of target districts for the Action, ensuring that Action’s contextually relevant <(>&<)> responsive to community-identified priorities <(>&<)> to different gender <(>&<)> groups. Oxfam <(>&<)> AJOAGO’s field experience, access <(>&<)> community acceptance directly informed of Action in WASH <(>&<)> Protection. Oxfam has coordinated sectors <(>&<)> locations with all responders to avoid duplication <(>&<)> make synergies. Oxfam will implement sensitive protection activities such as GBV case management, while partner doing WASH <(>&<)> protection awareness. Site <(>&<)> beneficiary selection, hygiene promotion <(>&<)> distribution is done jointly. Oxfam supports AJOAGO through sub-granting arrangement, technical guidance (incl. on WASH, Infection Prevention <(>&<)> Control, <(>&<)> Protection), financial mgt support, procurement support for WASH supplies <(>&<)> Dignity items, <(>&<)> monitoring <(>&<)> accountability mechanisms, ensuring delivery in line w/ Sphere <(>&<)> cluster guidance. To maximize impact <(>&<)> synergy, Action makes referrals to other responders. Oxfam will coordinate Action w/ DRA via several comms channels <(>&<)> monthly meetings; it meets AJOAGO weekly.
Action is informed by RNA, Oxfam <(>&<)> AJOAGO's community-based hum. experience <(>&<)> builds on ongoing coordination w/ DRA, UN, (I)NGOs <(>&<)> community leaders to avoid duplication <(>&<)> respond effectively to urgent flood needs, compounded by existing vulnerabilities in 3 hard-to-reach districts (Mabalane, Mapai, Massangena) in Gaza Province Action reaches 20,300 ppl w/ WASH, FSL <(>&<)> Protection. WASH <(>&<)> Protection are funded by DRA; FSL is funded by Oxfam own funding WASH: Action distributes 2400 hygiene kits; rehabilitates 20 damaged water points; builds capacity of 20 water mgt committees; tests water quality, cleans <(>&<)> disinfects 30 flood-contaminated water sources; distributes 3K water purifiers in areas w/ diarrhea <(>&<)> cholera outbreaks; <(>&<)> promotes hygiene. Infection Prevention <(>&<)> Control (IPC) <(>&<)> protection is integrated in allactivities in line w/ Sphere <(>&<)> WASH Cluster stds. Protection: Action strengthens community-based protection mechanisms in IDPcenters <(>&<)> communities through integrated sensitization, service mapping, referrals <(>&<)> PSS support. Sensitization is conducted on protection risks, GBV prevention <(>&<)> response, <(>&<)> legal rights, incl. info on available services <(>&<)> pathways to access or replace lost civil documentation Service mapping is conducted/updated in coordination w/ gov, NGOs <(>&<)> CBOs, Protection Cluster. Referrals are provided to at risk inds. to access specialized services (e.g. GBV, legal aid). Community members are supported through community structures <(>&<)> mobile protection teams to deliver PSS <(>&<)> Psychological First Aid in transit centers <(>&<)> communities To address immediate needs, 750 dignity kits are distributed to women <(>&<)> girls. Context-appropriate comms materials are disseminated. Activities are in line w/ Protection Cluster Stds. Gender is mainstreamed throughout, guided by Oxfam GiE framework <(>&<)> informed by a rapid gender analysis. Action is linked to early recovery <(>&<)> longer-term dev. to restore essential services <(>&<)> safeguard rights/dignity of affected communities.
